name: No Overtaking Line

plainEnglish.en: A single solid white line down the middle of a two-way road means stay on your own side and do not overtake.

formalMeaning.en: Where a single continuous solid white line separates traffic travelling in opposite directions, a driver may not drive on the right side of it and no part of the vehicle may cross it. Three narrow exceptions apply, and only when it is safe to do so.

behaviour.en: Keep left of the line and complete any overtaking before it begins. You may cross it only to enter or leave property on the other side, or to get past a stationary obstruction in the road, and only when it is safe.

commonMistake.en: Learners assume a solid line can never be crossed for any reason. It bans overtaking, but you may still turn across it into or out of a property when it is safe.

testHint.en: Expect a question on the three exceptions, and on whether you may turn right across it (yes, to reach or leave property). It is white, continuous, and at least 100 mm wide.

memoryTrick.en: Single Solid = Stay on your Side. Only property or a parked obstruction lets you touch it.

confidence: VERIFIED: name, white colour, single continuous solid line min 100 mm, all three exceptions plus the 'safe to do so' proviso read directly from SARTSM Vol 1 pp. 7.2.5-7.2.6.

name: No Crossing Lines

plainEnglish.en: Two solid white lines side by side are a wall: no overtaking and no turning across them.

formalMeaning.en: Two continuous solid white lines, each at least 100 mm wide. A driver may not drive on the right side of them and no part of the vehicle may cross them, unless passing a stationary obstruction in the roadway and it is safe to do so.

behaviour.en: Do not overtake, and do not turn right across the lines into or out of a side road or driveway. The only reason to cross is a stationary obstruction blocking the road, and only when safe.

commonMistake.en: Carrying the property-access exception over from the single no-overtaking line. Double lines are stricter: they ban the turn as well as the overtake.

testHint.en: The classic trap is one line versus two. One line still permits access to property; two lines permit only passing a stationary obstruction.

memoryTrick.en: Two lines, two bans: no overtaking AND no crossing.

confidence: VERIFIED: §7.2.6 'No Crossing Lines'. Sole exception is 'to pass any stationary obstruction in the roadway' — the manual does NOT say 'stationary vehicle'.

name: Left Edge Line

plainEnglish.en: The solid yellow line along the left edge marks the shoulder, and the shoulder is not a lane for you to drive in.

formalMeaning.en: A continuous solid yellow line at least 100 mm wide marking the left edge of the roadway. On a roadway with more than one lane in either or both directions a driver may not drive on the shoulder to its left, may not use that shoulder to overtake, and must make every reasonable effort to move fully left of the line for an emergency stop.

behaviour.en: Keep to the right of the yellow line. On a road with one lane in each direction you may move onto the shoulder to let a faster vehicle pass, but only between sunrise and sunset, only if you endanger nobody, and only when people and vehicles are clearly discernible at least 150 m away.

commonMistake.en: Treating the yellow line as a permanent slow lane. Driving on the shoulder is prohibited by default, the courtesy move is a narrow daytime exception, and you may never overtake on the shoulder.

testHint.en: The numbers get asked: yellow, minimum 100 mm, sunrise to sunset, 150 m visibility, and only while you are being overtaken.

memoryTrick.en: Yellow = Yield space, not Your lane. Daylight + 150 m + being overtaken is the only time you may borrow it.

source: SARTSM Vol 1 §7.2.8; NRTR 2000 reg 298A(1)-(2), reg 298(1) proviso
confidence: VERIFIED: RM4.1 IS the LEFT EDGE LINE, solid yellow min 100 mm (§7.2.8.2); RM4.2 is the RIGHT EDGE LINE and is white. The 'being overtaken / daytime / 150 m' duty is NOT in §7.2.8 — it is reg 298A(2), which ALSO requires the road be designated for one lane each direction (client omitted this).

name: Painted Island

plainEnglish.en: The painted area filled with yellow diagonal stripes is out of bounds: do not drive on it, stop on it or park on it.

formalMeaning.en: A white boundary line or lines enclosing yellow sloping bars in a diagonal or chevron pattern. No part of a vehicle may cross the marking, and no vehicle may stop or park on it, except when directed by a traffic officer or in the case of an emergency.

behaviour.en: Pass it on the correct side and keep every wheel off the paint. Enter it only on a traffic officer's direction or in a genuine emergency.

commonMistake.en: Using a painted island as a waiting space for a gap, or clipping its corner while turning. Both are offences even though the island is only paint.

testHint.en: There are exactly two exceptions: a traffic officer's direction and an emergency. Note that stopping and parking are banned too, not just driving over it.

memoryTrick.en: Stripes mean no-go. Only an Officer or an Emergency gets you on.

confidence: VERIFIED: §7.2.9.1 lists only TWO exceptions — traffic officer's direction, and emergency. 'To avoid a collision' is NOT a separate exception (client listed three).

name: Mandatory Direction Arrows

plainEnglish.en: A yellow arrow painted in your lane is the only direction you are allowed to take from that lane.

formalMeaning.en: Yellow arrows (variants RM8.1 to RM8.6) marked in a lane on the approach to a junction. Drivers may proceed only in the direction the arrow indicates.

behaviour.en: Read the arrow early and get into the correct lane well before the junction. Once you are in the lane, take only the direction shown, even if the queue next to you is shorter.

commonMistake.en: Treating the arrow as a suggestion, or changing lanes at the last second. The direction is compulsory, and the warning arrows further back are your cue to move over.

testHint.en: Colour is the trap: these arrows are yellow, not white. Six directions exist — left, left-or-straight, straight, right-or-straight, right, and right-or-left.

memoryTrick.en: Yellow arrow, no choice: follow the point.

confidence: VERIFIED: §7.2.12.2 states the arrows 'shall be marked in yellow' — the client said WHITE, which is wrong and is a likely exam question.

name: Traffic Circle Mandatory Direction Arrows

plainEnglish.en: At a mini circle, three yellow arrows and a painted circle tell you to go round clockwise, keeping the circle on your right.

formalMeaning.en: Three yellow arrows marked around a painted circle at a mini circle, imposing a mandatory requirement to proceed only in the direction the arrows indicate. Where the circle is painted rather than raised, drivers must not encroach on it, fully cover it, or pass to the right of it.

behaviour.en: Follow the arrows clockwise around the circle so it stays on your right. Do not drive straight over the painted circle or turn in front of it.

commonMistake.en: Driving over a mini circle because it is flat paint, or cutting right in front of it when turning right. Both break the mandatory direction.

testHint.en: Learn the colours and the direction: arrows yellow, outer circle white, inner circle yellow, and you travel clockwise with the circle on your right.

memoryTrick.en: Clockwise, circle on your right. Never cut the clock in half.

confidence: VERIFIED: §7.2.19.1 mandatory duty + 'not encroach / not fully cover / not pass to the right'; §7.2.19.3 clockwise. RM15 is the ARROWS, not a raised circle (client wrong). Paired sign R22 not yet in the library.
